design_detail: Randomized, double-blind crossover trial of two active stimulants without a placebo condition, run within a trial of their relative efficacy whose efficacy results are not reported in this paper. 125 children aged 5 to 15 years with DSM-IV ADHD, referred to a hospital behaviour clinic in Melbourne, took dexamphetamine (DEX) 0.15 mg/kg per dose and methylphenidate (MPH) 0.3 mg/kg per dose twice daily for 2 weeks each in random order, with a 24-hour washout. Parents rated 17 listed complaints on Barkley's Side Effects Rating Scale (0 = absent, 1 to 9 = severity) before treatment and at the end of each fortnight. The amphetamine studied is dexamphetamine alone.
can_establish: Within the same children, at these two fixed doses given twice daily for two weeks each, how parent ratings of 17 listed complaints differed between dexamphetamine and methylphenidate under randomized order and double blinding, and how often each complaint was already reported before treatment.
cannot_establish: Whether either drug causes or relieves a complaint compared with a dummy pill (there was no placebo, so drug-versus-baseline contrasts are unblinded and mixed with time, expectation and regression to the mean); whether the two doses were equally effective (efficacy is not reported here beyond parents' global ratings), so a difference between the drugs may reflect the 1:2 dose ratio chosen; effects after two weeks, at other doses or schedules, in adolescents, adults or girls (11 of 125), or with non-medical use.

sample.recruitment: Clinic: ambulatory patients referred to the Royal Children's Hospital, Melbourne, for ADHD assessment by paediatricians, family practitioners, school nurses or psychologists, or by parents themselves; enrolled April 1995 to August 1996 (p. 663).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Age 5 to 15 years; DSM-IV ADHD on the DuPaul rating scale (a symptom counted only if rated often or very often); T score at least 1.5 SD above the mean on the Attention Problems scale of the Child Behavior Checklist or Teacher Report Form; no intellectual disability, gross neurological abnormality or Tourette's syndrome; a clinical decision to try stimulant medicine (p. 663).
sample.demographics: 114 boys and 11 girls; mean age 104.8 months (SD 27.6; range 60 to 179), about 8.7 years (editors' conversion); mean estimated IQ 98.9 (SD 13.8); 101 of mixed type (printed as 81.8%; see reporting issues), 22 (17.6%) predominantly inattentive, 2 (1.6%) predominantly hyperactive-impulsive; mean Child Behavior Checklist attention-problems T score 75.9 (SD 8.4) (p. 663).
sample.attrition: Four children (3.2%) stopped one trial period because of severe adverse effects, two on each drug (p. 664). How their ratings for that period were handled is not stated; the degrees of freedom of the F tests (2, 122) imply 124 children in the analyses (editors' inference; see reporting issues).
sample.selection_effects: Referred clinic sample in whom treatment had already been decided, 91% boys, mostly of primary-school age; prior stimulant treatment is not reported. Parents who had sought an ADHD assessment made all the ratings, and the authors suggest some may have over-reported symptoms at baseline (p. 664). One hospital in one country.

exposure.measurement: Assigned by the investigators: both drugs as crushed powder in identical opaque gelatin capsules (p. 663); adherence was not measured or reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: dexamphetamine 0.15 mg/kg per dose and methylphenidate 0.3 mg/kg per dose, rounded to the nearest capsule size (2.5 and 5 mg capsules for DEX, 5 and 10 mg for MPH), by mouth twice a day after breakfast and after lunch, for 2 weeks each with a 24-hour washout between (p. 663). The authors call the doses moderate and note that other doses and spacing might give different side-effect profiles (p. 666).
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable (children). Other medicines are not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable. Baseline ratings were made before any trial medicine; drug ratings at the end of each 2-week period while it was being taken.

comparison.controls: Within-person: each child on the other drug (randomized order), and the same child's pre-treatment baseline. No placebo condition.
comparison.matching: Self-controlled crossover; order and period effects are not reported.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not an issue for the dexamphetamine-versus-methylphenidate contrast (within-person, randomized order). For contrasts with baseline, change over time, parents' expectations and changed perception of the child, and regression to the mean cannot be separated from drug effects; the authors raise the first two possibilities themselves (p. 664).

outcomes.instruments: Barkley's Side Effects Rating Scale (SERS), presented to parents as a behavior questionnaire to disguise its purpose: 17 items (trouble sleeping, poor appetite, irritability, proneness to crying, anxiousness, sadness/unhappiness, headaches, stomachaches, nightmares, daydreams, talking little with others, uninterested in others, drowsiness, biting fingernails, unusually happy, dizziness, tics or nervous movements), each scored 0 (absent) or 1 to 9 (severity), completed by parents at baseline and at the end of each fortnight (pp. 663–664). Efficacy measures were collected (Conners teacher and parent scales, Continuous Performance Test, parents' global ratings) but are not reported except parents' global improvement (p. 663).
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors state that no normative data have been published for the SERS and that no normed questionnaire for stimulant side effects exists (p. 663).
outcomes.operationalization: A genuine side effect: a complaint both more frequent (McNemar test) and more severe (repeated-measures ANOVA) on a drug than at baseline (p. 665, Discussion, 8th paragraph). Drug comparison: dexamphetamine-versus-methylphenidate contrasts on the number of complaints, their mean severity and the severity of each item.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Partial: the significance level was set at 0.01 because of the number of comparisons (p. 663); no formal correction across 36 measures (2 summary measures, 17 prevalence and 17 severity items) with up to 3 pairwise contrasts each.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Investigators, families, children and teachers were blind to the order throughout (p. 663). Baseline ratings were made off medication and could not be blinded. Blinding was not checked.

analysis.effect_sizes: Number of complaints (Table 1, p. 664): baseline 8.19 (SD 3.97), DEX 7.64 (3.83), MPH 7.19 (3.82); F(2,122) = 3.72, p = .03; only baseline versus MPH significant at p < .01. Mean severity of the complaints reported: 4.08 (1.56), 3.73 (1.68), 3.24 (1.46); F = 15.98, p < .01; baseline versus MPH and DEX versus MPH significant. Editors' calculation: DEX minus MPH mean severity 0.49 points on the 1-to-9 scale, about 0.31 of the pooled SD (ignoring the within-child correlation, which the paper does not give). Prevalence (Table 2, p. 664): poor appetite 43 (34%) at baseline, 74 (59%) on DEX, 69 (56%) on MPH; trouble sleeping 67 (54%), 88 (70%), 79 (64%). Item severity means (Table 3, p. 665; no SDs printed), baseline, DEX, MPH: trouble sleeping 2.21, 3.61, 2.69; poor appetite 1.22, 2.74, 2.12; irritability 4.57, 3.65, 2.94; proneness to crying 3.35, 3.4, 2.7; anxiousness 3.94, 2.71, 2.07; sadness/unhappiness 2.86, 2.43, 1.69; nightmares 1.09, .79, .48. Item means below 1 show that Table 3 averages include children without the complaint, scored 0 (editors' inference).
analysis.covariates: None. Repeated-measures ANOVA (Hotelling's multivariate test) with planned pairwise contrasts, and McNemar tests for prevalence (pp. 663–664); period and order effects were not analysed or reported.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol is mentioned (trial run 1995–1996).
analysis.selective_reporting: The efficacy results of the same trial are not reported here (p. 663). Table 3 gives no SDs or confidence intervals; prevalence contrasts between DEX and MPH are not shown (Table 2 marks only contrasts with baseline); period and carryover effects are not reported.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Parents already reported many of the 17 listed complaints before treatment (for example irritability in 82% and anxiousness in 77% of children). Compared with baseline, poor appetite was more frequent and more severe on both drugs, and trouble sleeping on dexamphetamine; most other complaints were reported less often or as less severe on the drugs. Dexamphetamine was rated more severe than methylphenidate overall (mean severity 3.73 vs 3.24) and on six items, mostly emotional ones, while the number of complaints did not differ between the drugs. Ratings were mostly in the mild part of the 0-to-9 scale, and four children stopped a period because of severe effects, two on each drug.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that both drugs caused appetite suppression, that dexamphetamine caused insomnia, and that many symptoms attributed to stimulants are pre-existing characteristics that improve with stimulant treatment (p. 662). The causal statements rest on unblinded comparisons with baseline, although the authors note that comparing with baseline may if anything understate side effects (p. 665). Improvement with treatment cannot be separated from placebo or time effects in a trial without a placebo, and the Discussion itself offers parental over-reporting before diagnosis and mothers' changed perception of the child as alternative explanations (p. 664). The comparison of the two drugs is randomized and blind but at one fixed dose ratio without shown equal efficacy, which the authors acknowledge (p. 666). The Discussion's statement that only trouble sleeping and irritability averaged above 3 on DEX overlooks proneness to crying (3.4 in Table 3) (p. 665).

timeline.event: Conners randomly assigned 75 children with minimal brain dysfunction to methylphenidate 30 mg, dexamphetamine 15 mg or placebo for 6 weeks: dexamphetamine produced significantly more side effects than methylphenidate, few of them moderate or severe (as summarized by Efron et al., p. 665; not read)

Pelham et al., random-order double-blind crossover in 22 boys: sustained-release dexamphetamine gave more adverse effects than the other preparations, not significantly, and severity was not reported (as summarized by Efron et al., pp. 665–666; not read)

Elia et al., crossover of methylphenidate and dexamphetamine at various doses in 48 boys: 83% had some side effects on both; decreased appetite 85% vs 95%, sleep difficulties 79% vs 81% (as summarized by Efron et al., p. 666; not read)
This trial: 125 children; dexamphetamine rated more severe than methylphenidate overall and on six items, with the same number of complaints

Network meta-analysis of double-blind trials: stopping because of side effects did not differ significantly between amphetamines and methylphenidate in children and adolescents (OR 1.60, 0.94 to 2.73, low certainty); its main text does not list its trials, so whether it includes this one is not known from the article

replication.where_it_stands: By its authors' account the largest direct comparison of the two drugs' side effects at the time (p. 666), in one clinic, at one dose ratio, for two weeks each, with parent ratings on a scale without norms. The network meta-analysis of Cortese et al. (2018) found no significant difference between amphetamines and methylphenidate in stopping because of side effects in children and adolescents; that outcome differs from rated severity, so it neither confirms nor contradicts this trial.

funding.funder: Dr Efron was supported by a Clinical Research Scholarship from the Royal Children's Hospital Research Foundation (Acknowledgments, p. 666). No other funding is stated, and the source of the study medicines is not stated.
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: All three authors from the Centre for Community Child Health and Ambulatory Paediatrics, Royal Children's Hospital, Melbourne (p. 662).

what_would_settle_it: A double-blind trial with a placebo condition comparing an amphetamine and methylphenidate at doses titrated to equal benefit, over months rather than two weeks, with a validated side-effect measure, absolute rates of each complaint and of stopping, and enough girls, adolescents and adults to describe them.

domains.note: Children were randomized to which drug came first (p. 663), but sequence generation and allocation concealment are not described and baseline characteristics by order are not reported.

domains.domain: Bias arising from period and carryover effects (crossover)
domains.note: A 24-hour washout between two 2-week periods, with ratings at the end of each period, makes carryover unlikely to dominate, but period and order effects were neither analysed nor reported.

Identical capsules and blinding of everyone involved (p. 663), but the blind was not checked and distinctive effects such as insomnia could reveal the drug; four children stopped a period early and how they were analysed is not stated.
The degrees of freedom imply 124 of 125 children in the analyses; who is missing, and what was recorded for the periods stopped early, is not stated.

Parent ratings on a questionnaire without norms (p. 663), made blind for the comparison of the two drugs. The baseline rating was made off medication and unblinded, so for contrasts with baseline this domain would be high.
No protocol or registration; all 17 items are tabulated, but between-drug prevalence contrasts, per-item SDs and the efficacy results of the trial are not reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: RoB 2 applies to the randomized comparison of dexamphetamine with methylphenidate, which is within-person and double-blind with identical capsules, with all 17 items reported. The concerns are undescribed randomization and missing-data handling, unexamined period effects, an untested blind and a parent-rated scale without norms; they are concerns of reporting more than of a likely direction of bias, so the overall judgment stays at some concerns rather than high. The contrasts of each drug with baseline are not randomized comparisons: without a placebo they are at high risk of bias and should not be cited as effects of the drugs. Cite for: at the study's doses (DEX 0.15 mg/kg and MPH 0.3 mg/kg twice daily) for two weeks each, parents rated dexamphetamine's complaints as somewhat more severe, mostly sleep and emotional items, with the same number of complaints and the same small number of children stopping. Do not cite for: effects against placebo, other doses, long-term use, adolescents or adults, or a comparison of strength between the drugs.

key_findings.finding: 125 children (114 boys, 11 girls) aged 5 to 15 years with DSM-IV ADHD, referred to a Melbourne hospital clinic, were enrolled between April 1995 and August 1996; mean age 104.8 months (SD 27.6).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Subjects, 3rd paragraph; Results › Sample Characteristics, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Design as conducted: randomized order of dexamphetamine 0.15 mg/kg per dose and methylphenidate 0.3 mg/kg per dose, twice daily for 2 weeks each, 24-hour washout, identical opaque capsules, with investigators, families, children and teachers blind; there was no placebo condition.

Before any medicine, parents reported irritability in 102 children (82%), anxiousness in 96 (77%), daydreams in 94 (75%), proneness to crying in 87 (70%), sadness/unhappiness in 85 (68%), trouble sleeping in 67 (54%) and poor appetite in 43 (34%).

Across the 17 items, the mean number of complaints was 8.19 at baseline, 7.64 on dexamphetamine and 7.19 on methylphenidate (only baseline vs methylphenidate significant), and did not differ between the two drugs; the mean severity of the complaints reported was 4.08, 3.73 and 3.24 (baseline vs methylphenidate and dexamphetamine vs methylphenidate significant).
key_findings.locator: Results › Total Side Effects: Prevalence and Severity, 1st paragraph (p. 663); Table 1 (p. 664)

key_findings.finding: Only two complaints were reported more often on a drug than before treatment: poor appetite on both drugs (59% on dexamphetamine and 56% on methylphenidate, against 34% at baseline) and trouble sleeping on dexamphetamine (70% against 54%; 64% on methylphenidate, not significant against baseline).
key_findings.locator: Results › Individual Side Effects: Prevalence, 3rd paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Compared with baseline, dexamphetamine increased the rated severity of trouble sleeping (mean 3.61 vs 2.21) and poor appetite (2.74 vs 1.22), and methylphenidate only that of poor appetite (2.12 vs 1.22); the drugs lowered the severity of other items, methylphenidate on eight and dexamphetamine on five.
key_findings.locator: Results › Individual Side Effects: Severity, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 664); Table 3 (p. 665)

key_findings.finding: Six items were rated more severe on dexamphetamine than on methylphenidate: trouble sleeping (3.61 vs 2.69), irritability (3.65 vs 2.94), proneness to crying (3.4 vs 2.7), anxiousness (2.71 vs 2.07), sadness/unhappiness (2.43 vs 1.69) and nightmares (.79 vs .48); no item was rated more severe on methylphenidate.
key_findings.locator: Results › Individual Side Effects: Severity, 2nd paragraph (p. 664); Table 3 (p. 665)

key_findings.finding: Four children (3.2%) stopped a trial period because of severe adverse effects, two on each drug (1.6% each). On dexamphetamine, an 8-year-old boy became overfocused, extra sensitive and increasingly anxious, and another 8-year-old boy agitated and uncharacteristically aggressive; both then took methylphenidate without problems. On methylphenidate, an 11-year-old girl had severe headaches soon after each dose and stopped after 4 days, and a 5-year-old boy became extremely aggressive and tearful; neither had major side effects on dexamphetamine. Each effect resolved immediately when the drug was stopped.
key_findings.locator: Results › Individual Side Effects: Severity, 3rd paragraph (left column, continuing at the top of the right column)

key_findings.finding: Parents rated most children as improved overall compared with their usual selves: 86 (68.8%) on dexamphetamine and 90 (72%) on methylphenidate; the paper does not otherwise report efficacy and does not test this difference.

Severity ratings were generally in the mild range of the 0-to-9 scale. The authors set the 1.6% per drug who could not tolerate it beside 3.6% and 1.9% in two earlier placebo-controlled methylphenidate trials, and cite Ahmann et al.: side effects also fell from baseline on placebo, so comparison with baseline may understate a drug's adverse effects.

The authors offer three explanations for complaints reported before treatment that fell on medication: parents seeking a diagnosis may have over-reported at baseline; the complaints may belong to ADHD itself and lessen with treatment; or mothers' globally negative view of a child with difficult behaviour may change once behaviour improves.

The authors attribute the extra insomnia on dexamphetamine to its longer half-life, and state that only moderate doses given twice a day were studied, that other doses and spacing might change the side-effect profiles, and that no child was younger than 5.

reporting_issues.issue: 101 children of mixed type are printed as 81.8%, and the three subtype percentages as printed add up to 101% (Results › Sample Characteristics, 1st paragraph). Editors' arithmetic: 101/125 is 80.8%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; the count (101) and the other two percentages fit n = 125.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says nightmares, stomachaches and anxiousness became less frequent on methylphenidate than at baseline, but Table 2 marks the baseline-versus-methylphenidate contrast for headaches (41% to 24%), not stomachaches (45% to 32%, unmarked); Table 3 likewise shows a significant contrast for headaches and none for stomachaches (p = .16).
reporting_issues.consequence: The word stomachaches in the text appears to be an error for headaches; claims should follow the tables.

reporting_issues.issue: Tables 1 and 3 report F statistics with 2 and 122 degrees of freedom, and neither a missing child nor the handling of the four periods stopped early is mentioned. Editors' inference: for a repeated-measures test across three conditions with Hotelling's test these degrees of freedom imply 124 children analysed, while 125 were enrolled (p. 663).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor for the results, but the analysed sample is not fully accounted for.

reporting_issues.issue: Three methylphenidate percentages in Table 2 are one point higher than their counts allow: trouble sleeping 79 (printed 64%), poor appetite 69 (printed 56%), sadness/unhappiness 69 (printed 56%). Editors' arithmetic: with n = 125 these are 63.2%, 55.2% and 55.2%, and no single denominator fits every row.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; claims should use the counts.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says only trouble sleeping and irritability averaged above 3, both on dexamphetamine, but Table 3 also shows proneness to crying at 3.4 on dexamphetamine.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor understatement of the severity of emotional complaints on dexamphetamine.

reporting_issues.issue: Headaches are marked as a significant baseline-versus-methylphenidate contrast in Table 3 although the F test for headaches is printed as p = .01, while significance was defined as p < .01.
reporting_issues.consequence: The headache contrast is borderline and should be treated as uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 gives item means without SDs or confidence intervals, and Table 2 shows no between-drug contrasts, so the size and precision of the six dexamphetamine-versus-methylphenidate differences cannot be computed.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims can give the means and the stated significance (p < .01), not effect sizes.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record, journal pages with a text layer), Pediatrics 100(4), pp. 662–666 (all pages, including the acknowledgments and references; text extracted and every number checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi, Table 2 also at 300 dpi). The file's first page is a publisher's cover page and its last page a publisher's information page, so printed p. 662 is PDF page 2. No supplement exists.
